item.text: {"question_id":"2B.1","answer":"During 2023, the record documents several formal Egyptian diplomatic initiatives in external crises: resuming GERD negotiations with Ethiopia and Sudan, hosting the Sudan-neighbors conference, convening the Cairo Peace Summit, agreeing with the United States on Rafah humanitarian access, and supporting ceasefire, civilian-protection, humanitarian-access, and two-state positions (BATCH-0016-E004; BATCH-0005-E005; BATCH-0021-E009; BATCH-0014-E008; BATCH-0015-E004; BATCH-0017-E005; BATCH-0021-E010). These establish presidential or governmental pursuit of diplomatic alternatives, but mostly record initiatives, stated aims, or agreements rather than proof that they preceded a specific force authorization, were subjected to cabinet or legislative scrutiny, or produced durable de-escalation. The GERD talks made no worthwhile progress, and the Gaza aid arrangement is documented only at an initial stage rather than as sustained implementation (BATCH-0016-E007; BATCH-0014-E009). In the Sudan crisis, Egypt’s June visa requirement made flight more difficult, while UN treaty-body findings and Amnesty later documented inadequate asylum safeguards, detention, and forced returns by Egyptian authorities; these are contrary evidence that available lawful and humanitarian alternatives were not consistently used, although the supplied record does not establish Sisi’s personal order or the sequencing of each operational decision (BATCH-0009-R07-E015; BATCH-0012-E020; BATCH-0001-E013). Overall, the evidence supports documented diplomatic activity but only a limited conclusion that peaceful alternatives were systematically pursued through formal decision processes before force; causal effects and personal attribution remain
